subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
The difficulty in dealing with this subject is just what i-3 indicated by my hon, friend from Peel (Mr. Blain). The hon. member for Maisonneuve introduced a measure which was very broad in its application, and in favour of which a large number of labour organizations sent out requests in various forms. But the difficulty is that during the time these organizations were considering the Bill as printed, the hon. gentlemen, after it was read a second time, produced amendments in committee which entirely alter its meaning, substance and effect. During the time this evolution was going on, the labour organizations and other public bodies were pouring in their requests on members to support the Bill. I must confess to my utter inability to understand whether these public organizations are endorsing the original Bill or the amended Bill. And, to complicate the matter still further, the government, apparently, is taken into the entire confidence of the hon. member who introduced the Bill. After the Bill was introduced, the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) admitted having seen the amendments, or certain of the amendments before they were read here by the hon. member (Mr. Verville). A little later, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) told us that, so far as he was concerned, he objected to the extension of the Bill to cover such public works as dredging and wharfs, showing that that hon. gentleman also had been taken into the confidence of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville). And, after the Bill has been caucussed and considered on the government side, tin 55
hon. member for Maisonneuve asks us for God's sake not to make a party matter of it. How are we to consider this Bill? It is difficult to say whether it is a matter of public interest or of party advantage that this Bill is before the committee. It is too important a matter to be played with in that fashion. It is a subject that has been before the country, and before this House for many years. I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Verville) when he says that the subject should be approached in a calm, judicial spirit, and without party bias, but with consideration only for the public interest and the interest of those whom it especially affects. But, how are we to consider the Bill in that light when, after the Bill is brought into the committee for consideration, after hon. members have consulted their constituents about it and have learned the opinions of those who are most interested, mey are confronted with a Bill which is entirely different and concerning which only part of the House has been informed? It was pointed out by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) when the Bill was last before the committee, that everything that was in the Bill, except a two hundred uoiiars' penalty could have been provided by the government by order in council. That position has not been met. The government could have dealt with the matter just as they dealt with the fair iwage clause in' the government contracts. It simply provides that in contracts to which the government is a party, labour should be; regulated in the manner specified in the Bill. That could all have been done by order in council.
But we must make the best of what we have. I would like to get information from the introducer of the Bill as to the opinion expressed by labour organizations, whether that opinion endorses the Bill as first introduced or the Bill as it is now. With that information, we should have some idea of what measure these organizations are asking for and supporting. I should like to move some amendments to * this section before it goes through. The sections already passed, I think, are entirely inappropriate in a Bill of this character. Had the Bill remained as drawn section 2 would have been appropriate, but it refers, in the great part, to something not now in the Bill. It shows exceptions to the application of the Act, but when you read the application of the Act under section 3, which is the only one left, there is no application to the matters excepted by section 2. Altogether, the measure has been drawn in such a manner and so hastily and ill-advisedly amended, that it is almost unintelligible. But, as I have said, we must make the best of what we have. I would suggest to the mover of the Bill-and would move it



if he adopts the suggestion-that section 3 be amended by inserting the words f or permitted ' immediately after the word ' required ' in line 26. The Bill provides that men shall not be required to work more than eight hours. But we all know that if the word ' required ' were the only one used in such a case, evasion would be so easy that the law would be practically powerless. An employer of labour can easily find pretexts and excuses under which the men would be practically compelled, though not ' required/ to work for longer hours. Unless the words ' or permitted ' are inserted, the Bill will be of little effect. I would ask the hon. member (Mr. Yerville) to consider that amendment. I shall have another one to suggest later on.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Under the Bill men are permitted to work more than eight hours, provided they are paid at least time and a quarter. I do not wish to go to the length of saying that a man shall not be permitted to work beyond certain hours. I do not think that would be fair, nor would anybody regard it as fair.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: There is no conscientious advocate of the nine-hour day or the eight-hour' day, who does not state distinctly that one reason why he advocates the limitation of hours is that more people may be employed and fewer left out of work. The hon. member (Mr. Verville) is violating the very foundation principle of the eight-hour day.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I guess I understand the proposition as well as the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) does.. When I state that sometimes men must work unusually long hours, I know; I have done work enough in my life to know about that. Circumstances sometimes arise under which work must be done speedily and yet you cannot put on two or three shifts a day. Men may have to put in a few hours extra to finish work within a certain time. And it would not be fair to put men, in such a case, in the position of violators of the law. That is the very reason why I provided in the clause that if men work beyond the hours specified, they shall be paid at least time and a quarter. That does not say they shall not be paid more. Some men now are actually paid time and a half or even double time for overwork. Some at the present time are working on single time, therefore I have put in the minimum number of hours. That is the reason why I struck out the word ' permit,' and replaced it with the word ' require,' because they are already permitted to work. Every hon. member in this House knows that there are cases which cannot be treated in any other way.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I understand the principle of 40 hours of labour per week in the same manner as it is understood by my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell), and I agree with him that the principle for which the workingmen of this country have been advocating would be destroyed if the grjel and selfishness of any individual labourer were allowed for the sake of earning an increased salary or emolument, to occupy the time that should be or might be given to other men in the same class of labour. I think that is really the principle, or one of the chief principles, which has been at the back of the agitation in favour of short suing the hours of labour. I am also satisfied that the numerous resolutions that many members of this House have received in the interest of labour refer, not to the Bill at present before the House, but to the Bill as originally introduced by the member for Maisonneuve. We also find that previous to the introduction of this Bill last session, a select committee had been appointed to investigate this subject, and authority rwas given to that committee, under the Minister of Labour, to employ expert counsel, and to get expert advice m the matter. We find that a very large sum of money has been expended, a large number of witnesses of all classes, both of those interested from a personal standpoint, and those representing the interest of labour, as well as employers of labour, have been heard before that committee, and there has now been brought down to us a book containing nearly 800 pages of evidence taken by that committee. I find, too, that that evidence has been summed up by a paid expert Prof. Skelton, who has been brought before this committee, and I presume that the Bill as introduced this session is based on his summary of that evidence. If not, what was the use of this large expenditu-e of time and money, if the Bill was not to be based on th-3 evidence before the committee? I think that is a reasonable position to take. Now, what was the evidence as placed before the committee and as) summed up by the expert whom the Minister of Labour employed, and in whom he seems to have had confidence? We find in this report a summing up of results, in various places and under various conditions, and this voluminous summing up, along with the voluminous evidence, fill, as I say, about 800 pages of this blue-book that I have before me. Let ms first quote from the evidence of Prof. Fisher, of Yale university, and see what he says in regard to these hours of labour. On page 315 the witness, speaking of Prof. Fishe:, says :
This commission was appointed to make a comprehensive investigation into the causes of deterioration or advance in national vitality.

And in regard to the working day, I would like to read an extract from Prof. Fisher's remarks. On page 45 he says: 'The present working day is a striking example of the failure to conserve national vitality. In order to keep labour power unimpaired, the working day should he physiological-i.e., it should be such as would enable the average individual to completely recuperate over night. Otherwise, instead of a simple daily cycle there is a progressive deterioration. A reduction in the length of the work day would be a chief means of improving the vitality of workmen, as well as the worth of life to them. The fatigue of workmen is largely traceable to their long work day and serves to start a vicious circle. Fatigue puts the workman in an abnormal frame of mind. He seeks to deaden his fatigue by alcohol, tobacco, exciting amusements, and excesses of various kinds. The momentary relief which he thereby obtains is purchased at the expense of an increasing susceptibility to fatigue, resulting sooner or later in complete depletion of his vital energies and in the contraction of tuberculosis or other fatal diseases. The decrease in the length of the working day has not diminished the output.
This is an extract from the report of Prof. Fisher of Yale university, who was appointed to investigate this question of shorter hours of labour, and it is on a par with the speech of the Minister of Labour, which the leader of the opposition referred to. Now, let us see what Prof. Skelton, the expert appointed by the governmenti says in r egard to it. On page 368 he speaks of the effect of Shorter hours of labour :
In the light of the experience of other countries m eight-hour legislation it may be pos-61 a e j'0 summai*ize briefly a few conclusions.
And first, as to the end proposed ? Men will answer this question differently, as they lay the chief stress on the making of men, or the making of goods, or the making of money. I rom the viewpoint of the social and cultural effects of shorter hours, there is little disagreement from the conclusion that a lessen-mg of the average hours now spent would make for good, in giving men more opportunity tor making the acquaintance of their families, more (Opportunity for self development and recreation, more opportunity for taking an intelligent interest in civic affairs. Undoubtedly with the minority the larger freedom will be abused, and the shorter day in the workshop means a larger evening in the saloon; yet few who question the wisdom of greater leisure on this ground would go the logical length of saying that the working day should be lengthened to cut off entirely the leisure that may be abused, especially in face of the undoubted fact that it is precisely long hours and exhausting toil which are the surest inducements to dissipation.
Then further, I will quote from page 361 :
Q. What was the date of the reduction to 54 hours?-A. I am not quite sure whether it was 1870 or 1871. The great reduction in hours came it may be noted with the increase in the price of coal in the early 70's; the wages, ad-55J	,
justed on a sliding scale basis rose so much that the men preferred to take some of the gain in shorter hours rather than in higher wages. It may be noted also that the average output per man per day was greatest in the. shortest hour districts.
So you see that one of the points which this gentleman was asked to inquire into, was the output of labour, and the expe.-t evidence given was that a reduction in the hours of labour would not result in a decreased output. We find the same result in the 'experience of the British War Office, where they employ a large number of men at strenuous labour. This is what Prof. Skelton says of that experience :
The results of this reduction are wholly favourable to the advocates of shorter hours. After eleven years trial, reports were sought from the two government departments chiefly concerned, and - were published by the Board of Trade in 1905. The War Office, the employees of which had been granted a reduction of 51 hours per week, stated that when the 48-hour week was first adopted it was anticipated that there would be a saving of time m stopping and restraining work at the breakfast hour, work not beginning till after breakfast under the new system, and also a saving of light and fuel.
It was also expected that a later hour of starting work would ensure greater regularity of attendance, that there would be an improvement in the physical condition of the men and an increase in their power of production. The fact that the reduction in the hours of work had not reduced the output, or increased the cost of it, in private factories in which the experiment had been tried, also led the War Office to assume that the cost of production would not be increased in their workshops. It is stated that these anticipations have been justified, and that it is clear that no extra cost has been incurred by the public on account of the reduction of hours, nor has the output of the work been diminished.
These quotations by experts after careful investigation of the experience of large employers of labour, are confirmed by reports of experience in Great Britain, Australia and other countries, and the conclusion reached is that shorter hours of labour, while improving the physical and social well being of the labourer, have not diminished the output, and have not increased the cost. Contracts for the erection, remodelling, construction or repair of all public works, such as post offices, custom houses, armouries, Intercolonial stations, freight sheds or locomotive equipment, wharfs, piers, breakwaters, railroads, canals, dredges, navy yards, arsenals,

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I regret that the Prime Minister has seen fit to endeavour to make a party question out of this matter by accusing hon. gentlemen on this side of the House of playing a game. There has been a game played here, but not by the opposition. We all remember what happened on the second reading of this Bill. As has been pointed out by the leader of the opposition, the gentleman who has made this Bill a special study-that is, the original Bill I am speaking of-moved the second reading by a speech in support of the Bill as printed and distributed, and of that Bill only; and the Minister of Labour allowed the motion for the second reading to carry. The hon. member who is in charge of such legislation, or of the cabinet's conscience in regard to such legislation, if it has a conscience, or of the government policy; if it has a policy, the Minister of Labour allowed that second reading of the Bill without a word of protest, the Bill as originally printed, the Bill that was before the House. Did he not commit himself to that Bill? Did he not distinctly approve of that Bill by allowing the second reading to carry, and the House going into committee? Then, as soon as he gets a chance, the Minister of Labour says-and I will not do violence to his language by shortly sum-rr arizing it-he said that he had discussed this matter with the hon. member for Maisonneuve, and because of some amendments that the member for Maisonneuve was willing to submit to, he, the Minister of Labour, was in favour of passing the Bill as it was going to be amended. The Minister of Labour was playing a game. Which side of the House has been playing the game, if there was one being played? It was the member of the cabinet particularly in charge of that sort of legislation who allows the Bill, as printed and distributed, the only Bill before the House, to pass its second reading, without any suggestion whatever that it did not suit him. He committed himself to that Bill in allowing that motion to carry'. Now that hon. gentleman has the temerity to stand up here and say that he proposes to ask the member who is in charge of the Bill, not to keep his agreement made between these two hon. gentlemen, but to withdraw the amendments which he, the Minister Of Labour, had stipulated for when he sat down and allowed the second reading to carry-playing a game upon this House, playing a game on the members of the opposition with regard to this Bill. And now the right hon. gentleman throws that aspersion upon this side of the House, that we have been playing a game, while we have

only diligently been trying to make this legislation suitable to the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman agrees with me, he approves of the statement that we have been diligently trying to improve this legislation. It was the -Minister of Labour who had made this secret agreement with the proposer of this Bili, which was to be carried out, and this House unanimously committed itself to something else, to the principle contained in the original Bill. And instead of the Prime Minister advising the committee to rise and see what could be done by the Minister of Labour and the member for Maisonneuve, instead of allowing other persons to come in and see what is behind this Bill, they, the government, are wasting the time of this House by this strange kind of proceeding. The Prime Minister sees fit to justify all that happened here by throwing an entirely unwarranted aspersion across the House that hon. gentlemen of the opposition have been playing a game in regard ta this Bill. Now, the Prime Minister ought to set an example in this House, and he ought to stand up and withdraw that expression. There is no warrant whatever for saying any such thing. The Bill was read a second time by the consent of the Minister of Labour. The Minister of Labour then said that he had only consented to it because he had a secret compact with the proposer of the Bill that certain amendments would be made, and the Minister of Labour says he was not in favour of the Bill which he voted for on the second reading unless those amendments were made.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.

I want to introduce in this country, as they have in other parts of the world, a measure providing that the eight-hour principle shall be applied to a certain class of works. I am not so particular about the amount of work that it is applied to, provided we have on the statute-book, as they have in other countries, a measure of this kind. I know that some hon. members are of opinion that the Bill is rather radical in some respects, and in so far as it respects individual concerns, I would be willing to go even beyond the Bill that I have before the House at the present time. But, of course, I also consider the application of that measure, and consequently I am anxious that it should pass not only this House but the Senate and become the law of the land. When the Bill is in committee, I shall present some amendments which I am sure will meet with the good will of members on both sides.
That is what the hon. member said in moving the second reading of the Bill. The second reading has to do with the principle of the Bill. Now I endorsed heartily every word the hon. member said, I endorsed the principle, and supported the second reading of the Bill. The information I had with regard to the amendments was such as any other hon. member could have had by asking for it. Yes, and I may include myself, because as the Bill was originally proposed I think it was too drastic. My hon. friend from Kootenay says he is in favour of the Bill as introduced, and if that be so he cannot object to the Bill as amended. He could say

that in his opinion the amended Bill does not go far enough, but that is no reason why he should not adopt the Bill as it is proposed. My hon. friend from Maison-neuve (Mr. Verville), as I understand, is acting as a member of the Labour Council and as a workingman and he thinks this Bill is a step in the right direction. He tells us very frankly that the Bill does not go as far as he would like it to go either in its amended form or in its primary form as introduced, but he says he is anxious to have the principle of an eight-hour-day consecrated into law in this country, and he tells us that he does not ask for more at this moment than that we should recognize that principle. It is no answer for hon. gentlemen on the other side to say that they would vote for this Bill if it went further or if it applied to this kind of labour or to that kind, because the question is whether we are in favour of the principle of the Bill. The House has affirmed by the second reading of the Bill that it is in favour of the principle and now we have supplied the application of the principle. My hon. friend from Maisonneuve has stated with very great frankness that this is a new principle in the social question, and one which is subject to very great objection in many quarters, and he tells us he will not go so far as he intended to go originally but that he will be satisfied for the present if the measure should be applied to gov4 ernment contracts, not of all kinds, but of certain kinds. That is tire question we have before us, and it seems to me we should proceed with the Bill as it is amended. If gentlemen on the other side think it is too restricted it is open to them to propose that the Bill should go further, but certainly the principle contained in it ought to be given effect to.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I do not uphold the principle that before this House passes any legislation it should appeal to the country or to those particularly interested for an opinion so as to shirk responsibility. But, I do say that when the Bill as originally introduced has been sent out to those interested for their opinion and has received the endorsation of those interested in labour, it is very unfair to bring in a Bill of this kind which is a totally different Bill altogether, and which has not in its present form been passed upon by the labouring people of this country. We all know that when the Insurance Bill was introduced the insurance people were invited to come here in a body and they were heard for weeks before a committee of this House. The same was the case with the Co-operative Bill and the Banking Bill and Bills of that kind applying to capital. I do not say that it is the duty of parliament to endeavour
to shift its responsibility in this way, but
1	do say most emphatically that the Bill was brought in with the recognition, at least, of the government, expressed through the Minister of Labour, and that Bill as originally introduced was sent out to the labour organizations of the country, and the members of this House have received letters from these various associations asking them to support that Bill. In view of that, is it not fair that when this emasculated Bill is introduced, which really does not grant the principle which the First Minister has contended for, that the labour organizations should have an opportunity of knowing of the change in the Bill and deciding whether or not they would ask members of parliament to support it in its present form? The hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) has made it quite clear that there is absolutely no principle in this amended .Bill at all. Think of the absurdity of the Minister of Labour standing up here this afternoon and telling us that subsection
2	of section 3 of the Bill is an independent clause and may be applied to every man employed in day labour. Why, that is merely a subsection, and if what the Minister of Labour said were true it should be and would be a separate section of the' Bill. This incident simply shows how little the Minister of Labour understands the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I have no doubt whatever that the labour organizations for which my hon. friend (Mr. Good-eve) seems to speak would prefer the Bill originally introduced in this House to the Bill in its amended form. But the Canadian people are not composed only of the working classes; there are other classes, and these other classes object to the Bill. I can understand very well that although the working classes would welcome this measure even if it were more drastic than when first introduced, still they realize that there are other interests to be considered, and they are willing, as is the case in regard to most of such legislation, to take the principle in an amended form and to accept less than they would like to have.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: How do you know they are willing to accept this amended Bill? That is the real point. The right hon. gentleman must know that the original Bill was placed before the people for their opinion and that this amended Bill was not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I take my opinion from the man who introduced this Bill, who is a workingman himself and who is a member of the labour organizations, and who is willing to take this amended form of the Bill in order, as he says, to make a beginning and introduce the prin-

ciple. I have no doubt whatever that if the workingmen thought they could get more they would seek to obtain it, but my hon. friend (Mr. Goodeve) knows that few reforms which have been achieved have been proposed just as they were conceived by those who proposed them. No reform has ever been introduced in any country as it was conceived by the mind of the re-fo-mer. These great reforms have to be brought on piecemeal. My hon. friend (Mr. Verville) introduced his Bill a few weeks ago, and I have cited the opinion of prominent members of this House who believe that it was altogether wrong to interfere in any way to prevent a man working as many hours a day as he wished. It is in view of all these objections that the mover of the Bill has agreed to amend it and to support it in its amended form. It is open for my hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) to say: I will have the Bill as it was first introduced. But, because the Bill is not as broad as my hon. friend (Mr. Verville) would wish to have it, that is no reason why the hon. member for Kootenay should oppose it altogether, if, as I conceive, he wants to be logical.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
When the Bill was first introduced I offered a few words to explain my attitude towards such legislation. I did not intend, nor did I in any way misdirect my intention, to offer any opposition to the Bill as originally proposed. To the principle of the eight-hour day, properly applied', I assent. To the Bill as introduced now I do not assent, because in it I see no principle whatever. The hon. Minister of Labour has been told by the parties who have urged the Bill that there is nothing of it left except a halting and faltering step in the direction they indicated and a halting and faltering step is always made by a halting and faltering government. The hon. minister says that no great reform ever comes excepting piecemeal. I think he will acknowledge that the abolition of the corn laws in Great Britain was a great reform; will he point out the piecemeal steps that led to the abolition of the corn laws? If there were a firm and manly step taken towards eight-hour labour, it would not be opposed by those who recognize the principle. But in this Bill there is no step at all. I cannot conceive of an eventuality in which the labourer is going to be assisted to eight hours labour by this Bill. If it were designated properly, it would be called, not an Act respecting the hours of labour on public works, but an Act to legalize overpay of government employees. Under this Act a man can make a contract to work eight or ten or twelve or as many hours as he pleases or as the employer can screw out of him. The conditions of labour are going to prevail just as they were before. The employer can go into the labour Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
market and ascertain what labour is being paid, and make any contract with his men that he can now make with them and is hampered by this Bill in no way whatever. It means just this, that men employed on government work and paid by the government shall be paid more than men employed on the same work by other parties, that is to say, it legalizes payment of men employed by the government at a higher rate than otherwise would obtain, and that applies only to day labour. If we are going to move in the direction of an eight-hour day, let us move sensibly. Let us apply the principle where it will do most good, let us apply it to the factories-to those conditions where long hours of labour are most oppressive, and to those classes of our population who can least stand long hours of labour. Let us have some rational principle behind it. Perhaps the Minister of Labour will remind us that most of these cases are beyond the jurisdiction of the government. Suppose that is true, let the same considerations prevail wherever the government has jurisdiction. But let us not have an irrational arbitrary Act such as this, applied only to those employed by day labour by the government. It would be as rational to enact that a man who works on the north side of a building should be employed eight hours while the man who works on the south side should be employed ten hours. It would be as rational to say that a man six feet high should work eight hours a day, while a man under six feet high should work ten hours. There is no principle in the Bill whatever. If the government will amend this Bill to make it mean something, to make it a logical start in the direction of eight-hour labour, I do not think it will meet any objection on this side of the House. I do not think the Prime Minister can point to a word uttered on this side of the House indicating that it will be opposed; but when he introduces a Bill based on no rational principle at all, tending not in the slightest degree to alleviate the conditions of the workingmen, he cannot expect it to be supported here.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: We have had from the Prime Minister an announcement a few moments ago that the government desires to stand behind the amendments in the form in which they are now before this committee, subject to such changes as may commend themselves to the wisdom of the committee. That being so, I wish to direct the right hon. gentleman's .attention to the amendment proposed to section 3. No matter what discussion takes place, we must admit that the language crystallized in the Bill will be the language that will voice what is done, it is not the speeches which hon. gentlemen may make here. Therefore, it is very essential to express accurately what we are enacting. The right hon. gentleman said that we are all practically committed to the principle of the measure, but that we differed as to the extent to which the principle should go. Now, this section provides that every contract shall contain a stipulation that ' no labourer, workman or mechanic shall be required to work more than 48 hours in any one week.' There is no law that requires any one to work, and if this provision is applied to every government contract, you will be affirming something that is meaningless. The workmen of this country sell their labour freely in the labour market, and unless you provide that no labourer, workman, or mechanic shall be ' required or permitted ' to work a certain number of days in the week or a certain number of hours per day, a contractor will be at perfect liberty to refuse to employ any man who will not work more than eight hours a day or 48 hours a week without violating this section. You must put something in that will prevent the contractor from compelling men to work more than the stipulated time, otherwise the clause is meaningless. I do not wish to support or oppose this Bill in silence. How are things to-day as they stand without this Bill? A contractor and a labouring man can enter into any agreement they choose, that the latter shall work for eight hours, or ten hours, or twelve hours, or six hours a day. subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
At six o'clock I was endeavouring to point out the utter futility of our enacting this measure with a view to assisting the workingmen in any way. I

find nothing within the four comers of this Bill, in fact, it is admitted by the promoters of the Bill that there is no provision in it restricting the hours of the day to eight. It is admitted that if this Bill were enacted the employer and employed would be in the very same position that they are to-day, that is, they could agree between themselves upon the number of hours that the workman should work in the day. It is true that one hon. gentleman opposite (Mr. Devlin) pointed out the provision in the latter part of section 3:
Additional hours if worked shall he classed as overtime and paid for at a rate of not less than time and a quarter.
If you look at it for one moment you will see there is nothing in it for the benefit of the workingman. Take an actual case. Suppose that the length of the day in the part of the country where a public building is being erected is 10 hours, and that the v/ages are $3 per day. A mechanic comes along and asks the employer for work. The employer says: Yes, I can give you work. What wages are you giving? Twenty-five cents an hour for the first eight hours and 50 cents an hour for the last two hours, which will make you $3 for the 10 hours. That will be strictly within the provisions of this Bill. If the wages be $2 a day the employer says to the labourer: I will give you 174 cents an hour for the first eight hours, which will be $1.40, and 30 cents an hour for the other two hours, the 9th and 10th.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: In all of the schedules attached to the government contracts fihe rates of wages are fixed at so much per hour, not so much per day. I think in assuming that the rate will be fixed at $3 a day the hon. member has no regard to the schedule of our contracts.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I am not familiar with the provisions to which the hon. member reiers.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: That is what I thought.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: But I fancy there is nothing in them to prevent just what I suggested.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Yes there is, that is just the point; the contract stipulates that the employer must pay a certain rate fixed in the schedule, that is, the rate under the fair wages resolution, which cannot be departed from by a contractor.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: We are at present simply discussing the provisions of this Bill. As I said, I am not familiar with any other provision but this Bill, so that there is nothing within the four corners of this Bill that could by any possibility be of any advantage to the worker. But we are told that it is desirable to establish a principle.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
What principle is there in this Bill? There is no principle in the Bill at all, if you confine yourself to the Bill itself. There is not the principle of eight hours to the day. That is not in this Bill, because it remains open, as I said, to the employer and the employed to make any bargain they choose as to the number of hours the workingman shall work. In order to protect the workingman you must make it prohibitive, that he shall not work longer than a certain number of hours per day, because without that you leave the employee, as he is to-day, or as some claim he is, at the mercy of the employer. That is the very thing that some of the workingmen desire to have done away with. There are workingmen who do not want this Bill at all, who want to be perfectly free to work as many hours as they choose, but I admit that many unions have agreed to support the Bill as originally introduced by my hon. friend from Maison-neuve (Mr. Verville). But there is no principle in this Bill at all. A principle is a rule or something of that kind that is to apply to all cases or certain classes of cases. If that is a fair definition of a principle there is no principle here. Even if for the sake of argument, it were to be admitted that eight hours a day is recognized in this Bill, it does not apply, this Bill does not propose it should apply, to any class of work except on public buildings. As a principle, I am opposed to an eight-hour day. I am very strongly opposed to it, and I know there are hundreds of workingmen in the city I represent who are opposed to it In the first place, I am opposed to it because it provides in many instances too many hours for a day's work. There are in my city many men working at kinds of work where I think they should not work more than four or five hours a day, that is before furnaces, in places -almost intolerable, hot, uncomfortable, unhealthy, exhausting. Four or five hours a day is quite long enough for men engaged in that kind of work. Therefore, I am opposed to fixing eight hours a day. I think it is too long. Eight hours is too long for a man to work in a mine, where he has no sunlight oi fresh air, or comfortable or healthy surroundings. Eight hours is too long for the glass blower to work. There are many kinds of work where I would be distinctly opposed to permitting men to work eight hours. There are other kinds of wiork where I should be opposed to restricting the time to eight hours. I quite agree with my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that it would not be wise to attempt to restrict the hours in farming operations to eight. My sympathies are and always have been with the toiling many, rather than with the privileged few, and I am quite anxious to do anything within reason, within the power of this House, to improve the lot of the

workingman, and if a Bill were thought out properly and certain hours fixed for certain kinds of work I would be most anxious to support it. Women and children are working too long in factories, but it is utterly impossible to apply an eight-hour day as a principle to all kinds of industry. I am opposed to this Bill because it does not promise any relief to the workingman, and there is nothing within the four comers of it, as I have said, that will tend to assist or help the workingman. I am opposed to the principle; I do not want to be tied up,
I do not want this Bill to be passed and then to have it said next year or two years from now: You agreed to an eight-hour day for that class of men. That is work that least demands interference on the part of this House. We all know that many, although not all, men employed on government work feel that it is perfectly legitimate to do as little work as possible and get as much pay as possible for that little work.
I believe, speaking generally, that they do less work than men who are employed by private employers. I, therefore, think you are beginning at the wrong end entirely in making any attempt to limit those who are in the service of the government on public buildings only to eight hours. Then, think of the confusion that would arise. A contractor having the erection of a public building would have to employ subcontractors, he would employ a subcontractor to do the tinsmithing, to put on the eave-troughs. The tinsmith has 15 or 20 men at work. The few working on the building, if there is anything in this Bill, which is very doubtful, would work only eight hours, while the men working on the adjoining, building might be working 10 or 12 or 14 hours. The Minister of Labour gave us a reason for the author of this Bill proposing these amendments, that the original Bill could not be carried in this House, but I have yet to learn that there is anything that cannot be carried in this House that has the support of the Prime Minister. To say that the original Bill could not be carried in the House is tantamount to saying that the Prime Minister would not support it.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: He said so himself.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
It seems to me that the government is responsible for the passage of every Bill that passes and for the rejection of every Bill that is rejected, and if the Prime Minister desired the original Bill to pass and thought it in the best interests of the working people of this country it was his duty to say so, and if he had said so there is no question but that it would have been carried. The right hon. gentleman tells us that he is in favour of this present Bill, which really does not amount to anything. I [DOT] do not want it to
be understood that the workingmen in my city are so wanting in intelligence as not to be able to see that this Bill is a delusion and a sham. If the author of the Bill, assisted by the Minister of Labour and perhaps by the Prime Minister, had deliberately set to work to submit a Bill to this House that was utterly useless as benefiting the workingman, they could not have succeeded better. I have become tired of the number of Bills that have been submitted to this House and passed with the apparent intention of humbugging people outside this House. We had the Anti Combines Bill of last year, which was of that character, and we have now this Bill, introduced apparently for the purpose of enabling the government to say to the workingmen of this country: We have tried to do something for you, we have passed an eight-hour Bill, while at the same time they know that this eight-hour Bill so called will be of no use whatever to the workingmen either now or in the future. There is no principle in it; there is nothing whatever in it to improve the present condition oi the workingman. I therefore have no hesitancy in opposing this Bill; I know that the workingmen in my city would oppose it if they were here, and for the reasons I have stated.

Mr. Speaker, it may be the result of my lack of experience, being one of the younger members of the House without much practical knowledge of the rules of parliamentary debate, without that wisdom which enables older members to take the proper means for forwarding their personal views, but I see no reason whatever for this protracted debate on the principle of a public Bill, which principle has been sanctioned by the House a few days past. I fallowed the debate closely this afternoon, and observed that it concerned itself entirely with the principle of the eight-hour day. Now, according to my interpretation of the rules of the House, as soon as a Bill has gone through its second reading, the principle of the Bill is thereby sanctioned by the House. It appears strange to me, therefore, that the hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Crothers) as well as those who preceded him this afternoon, should assert that there is no principle whatever involved in the Bill. That looks very much like giving one's self a certificate of inconsistency, seeing that they never uttered a word of protest when the Bill was brought up for its second reading.
It is contended that theTe is no principle whatever contained in the Bill now before the committee. Well, in the original Bill there was at least this principle involved that any man employed by the government, either on contract or by the day,

could not be held to work for more than eight hours a day. Hon. gentlemen on the other side opposed this Bill, and its promoter for it should be observed that this is a public and not a government Bill- the promoter of the Bill, who is at liberty to do whatever he pleases under the circumstances, stated this afternoon that he was ready to withdraw the amendments he had introduced. Now, what did these hon. gentlemen opposite then do? They did not take up his proposal, as they were intent on getting a statement of the governments views in connection with this Bill which is not a government measure.
One cannot fail to see that hon. gentlemen opposite have been trying to make political capital out of this discussion. It seems to me that whenever a private member introduce a Bill having for its object the promotion of the public weal, hon. members on the opposition as well as on the government side should cast aside all party considerations and take up the Bill solely on its merits. Far from taking such a stand, hon. members on the other side, as I noticed, have been constantly trying to induce the right hon. leader of the government and the hon. Minister of Labour to state the government's views in this connection. The hon. Minister of Labour stated _ that the government would (accept the Bill as amended. What more is required?
I understood on behalf of the opposition
at least that is what I gathered from the utterances of one or two of its members- that if the promoter of the Bill agreed to withdraw the amendments submitted by him and introduced anew the original Bili, they would be willing to support it. subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
We have had this Bill before the House a number of times. I remember it in the last two sessions, and I believe it was here a considerable time

before I came to this House; and it seems to me that every time it comes before the House it is in a worse condition than before. Last year it had in it a good many things that are not in it now. Its promotor was prepared to introduce an eight hour day for everybody in connection with government works. That is to say, if a man who had a factory entered into a contract with the government, he would have to put everybody in his factory under the eight hour system in order to comply with the Bill. Objection was taken to that. I do not think any of the members who desired to vote for the Bill wanted a provision of that kind in it. But the principle we did adopt was that the Bill should apply to all government works, whether carried on by the government itself or by contract with the government that all construction works in connection with railways, canals, public buildings or other kinds of public work. That is the principle I stand by to-night. The reason the Bill was withdrawn last session was simply that some of the lawyers said that it was not very well worded. I said at that time that I believed we could rectify the wording of the Bill in committee, so as to make it fulfil what was intended. Before this session we were accustomed to only one father for this Bill; but this session there came suddenly a stepfather in the person of the Minister of Labour, and this afternoon wre discovered another father, a foster father, in the person of the Prime Minister. He had to take up the Bill because the other two fathers became very weak or neglectful, and he undertook to help them out of the difficulty. The right hon. gentleman say this is a class Bill. I do not call it a class Bill at all; if it were, I would not support it. This is a Bill for the masses, not the classes. It is a Bill to protect the workingmen. As the Minister of Labour said, we have to get all reforms piecemeal, to get in the thin end of the wedge, and there is no better place to put in the thin edge end of the wedge for the eight hour day than in the public works of the country. Who are the men who have built and are keeping up the public works of this country but the masses? Who sent us to this parliament but the masses?-and 1 hope that when some of these hon. gentlemen appeal to these masses, they will be treated as they have treated the masses in connection with this Bill. The principle of the Bill is all right. Few hon. members know how eloquent the hon. Minister of Labour can be if they have not had the opportunity of hearing him before boards of trade and other bodies throughout this Dominion when he is not held responsible for what he says. On such occasions he is prepared to say almost anything on behalf of labour. But to-day
he tells us distinctly that if a workman wants to work only eight hours a day he will be paid for only eight hours. On other occasions the hon. gentleman waxed eloquent over the poor workingman who only saw his wife once in a while and his children never, and she did not know why, and he wanted to cut down the hours of labour in order that that man might have an opportunity to go home and see his wife and children. I want an eight hour day which will be eight hours and no more on public works, and I want men to be paid a decent wage for those eight hours, so that they will be able properly to support their families. The hon. Minister of Labour should be ready to stand by his guns and back up that principle. It would be interesting if the Minister of Public Works would give us the reasons for his opinion that the second clause of section 3 would apply to anything else than a public building.
The provisions of this section shall, as respects the hours of labour, apply to work undertaken by the government by day labour.
Now the provisions of this section apply only to public works, and how any court of law could interpret that as applying to any other works, passes my comprehension. Now, I think if the Minister of Labour will only reason with me for a moment, I can , convince him that there is nothing whatever in this Bill as to the hours of labour. He has already acknowledged that there is nothing in this Bill to prevent any man working more than eight hours, or more than ten hours; there is nothing to prevent him doing so of his own election, or to prevent him contracting to do so with a contractor. Now, the Minister of Labour comes back and says that if he does work more than eight hours he must be paid time and a quarter. Very well, he can still work just as long as he is told to do, and if he does not he can be fired, just as he could before. The Minister of Labour says; Read that in connection with the regulations, with the conditions the government insert in their contract schedules, that the workmen shall receive the hourly wage current in the district. He says if you read that in connection with this clause you will find that they must be paid the same wages as they were before for the eight hours, and a time and a quarter for the two hours. Well, suppose they, are, what does that amount to? It simply amounts to a change in the schedule. If you add a change in the schedule and say that they shall be paid current wages in the district and five per cent more, then you have got the whole Bill-and that is the Minister of Labour's own interpretation. Nothing to prevent a man working more, nothing to prevent him contracting to work more than eight hours. But the minister says there is a clause under which the government contractor shall pay five per cent more than current wages. Now, I put it to the Minister of Labour

again. Is there any possible result to work out of that Bill except to give the labouring man five per cent more, according to his own interpretation, than the current wages in the district? There is nothing. Now the Minister of Labour says that it would be grossly unjust to the people of this country, of whom this parliament are the trustees, to pay to a labouring man more than he earns, and if you pay him for more than eight hours, when he has only worked eight hours, you are robbing the people. But that is what this Bill does, if it has any effect at all, it is going to pay the labouring man five per cent more than the current wages.
I presume the schedules of the department are founded on the theory that the current wages in the district are what the man actually earns and therefore are paid. He has been paid that hitherto, he has always been paid it. If this Bill has any affect it is to add 25 per cent more to his wages for the last two hours which means 5 per cent more on the whole day of 10 hours. Therefore, to that 'extent we are robbing the people of 5 per cent and are not affecting the hours of labour at all. That is the whole result of the Bill. I have given it careful thought and I know, I am confident the Minister of Labour cannot say it has any other effect as to the hours of labour, it is merely a fetich or as the member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) said, a humbug, and I conceive that this House does not sit here to humbug the labouring man or any class. If the Bill means any progress, even a hair's breadth, towards assisting the labour man, let us all support it. If it means nothing at all, or worse than nothing, 5 per cent robbery in the words of the Minister of Labour, then let us not support it. Surely it is the duty of the Minister of Labour, unless he caii show that the Bill means something towards affecting the hours of labour, which he cannot show, it is his duty to withdraw the Bill in its present amended form. We were told this afternoon that it is only getting in the thin end of the wedge, if it works well we will carry it farther. What does that mean? That if the workingmen are satisfied to surrender to the government their liberty we will buy them with a bribe of 5 per cent more than they ordinarily earn when they work on a public building, and if we find they express satisfaction with that, we will extend it further and go into the treasury a little more and pay them more than they earn on other works over this country. That is all it means. The Prime Minister tells us we must get such reforms by piecemeal. I have read history to disadvantage if we get reforms of this kind by piecemeal. It is quite true the education of the people up to the reform proceeds by slow degrees, it is a matter of slow and patient teaching ;
but when the reform comes, if it is a bold and manly reform, it comes usually at one fell swoop from bold and manly "men. I have never yet seen a reform come, and I challenge the minister to look over the history of any country and find a reform introduced by an anaemic spectre such as he leads across the stage to-night. It has ne effect unless to take out 5 per cent from the treasury and to bribe the workingman by paying him 5 per cent more than he earns.

As a matter of principle I believe in the eight-hour day. Some members are disposed to support a Bill of this kind because they are called upon to do so by labour organizations in their constituencies. As a matter of fact, if a measure could be devised, and it was within the power of this House to pass such an Act, to give effect to a universal eight-hour day for labouring men throughout the whole Dominion, I would support it because I believe in it as a matter of principle. I believe in it first because I believe it would bring up a mors rugged, a stronger, a better class of labouring men in the country, who would be better citizens, better assets of the country. If the eight-hour day were applied, if workingmen were well housed and properly fed, I believe we would have far more efficient work performed than from the same men to-day working 10 hours.
Coming down to this Bill, I am disposed to agree with the hon. member who has just preceded ms (Mr. Meighen), and also with the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) who says it is a delusion and a sham. So far from this being a Bill affecting the hours of labour upon public works, it could with equal correctness be called an Act to incorporate a railway to run from the earth to ths moon. There is nothing whatever within the four corners of the Bill which could in any degree entitle it to be called a Bill in favour of an eight-hour day. It has been suggested that there is if noi some provision in the Bill to bring about an eight-hour day, at least some measure of relief to the workingman inasmuch as it may cause him to get a little increased wage if he works two hours over the eight hours. Here I agree again with the hon. member for West Elgin, who effectually disposed of that view by showing that the employer has it in his power to make ths pay sufficiently less during the eight hours, to make it the same as it was before for the whole day. But assuming for the sake of argument that this Bill was designed to give an eight-hour day to labouring men employed on public buildings, I cannot conceive of any logical reason being advanced why the benefit of this measure should be given to a man working on a government building

and be denied to a government employee -working in two or three dozen other capacities, which were indicated specifically jn the Bill as originally introduced in this House by the hon. member for Maison-neuva (Mr. Verville).
In common with other members of the House I have received a great many communications from different labour organizations expressing their approval of the Bill as originally submitted, and asking my support. I think without question that all of these letters were written after the original Bill had been submitted to the various unions. The amendments to this Bill were affected, I shall not say in a secret way, but at all events in a somewhat peculiar way, inasmuch as after the Bill was read a second time and thereby received the endorsement of this House as to its principle, certain amendments were suggested in the committee, and it was decided subsequently to reprint the Bill and have it brought down and this was done, the introducer of the Bill (Mr. Verville) working in collaboration with the Minister of Labour. But it has reached the ears of certain other government employees that it was proposed to very much restrict the operations of the Bill. In evidence I have the following letter :
Moncton, N.B., Dec. 28, 1910.
E. N. Rhodes, Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-We the undersigned, representing organized labour in the city of Moncton, hereby enter an emphatic protest against the proposed amendments to the Eight-hour Bill (known as Bill No. 3), which amendments, if passed, will utterly eliminate from its benefits the thousands of employees of the government on the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island railways. We particularly object to the striking out of section 5 of the Bill.
We believe that in the matter of hours and wages and in ideal working conditions generally, the government of the country should be the leader, not the follower. To this end we would urgently request your support to the Bill as originally proposed.
Thanking you in advance for any support you can render us at this time, we remain, Tours very truly,
Trades and Labour, Council-

My hon. friend's amendment is one calculated to defeat the object of this Bill. This is, I think, an advanced measure; it is one decidedly in the interest of the labouring people of this country. It is affirming a principle for which the working people have been contending for a long time, and it will be moving a great step in the way of meeting their wishes. My hon. friend as a lawyer surely would agree with me that on a compldint made before a magistrate that a workingman had been required to work more than 48 hours a week without an emergency having arisen, it would be for the magistrate to decide whether an emergency had arisen or not; and the Summary Convictions Act provides a cheap and expeditious mode of proceeding. subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: The House resumed the adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. Lancaster for the second reading of Bill (No. 2) to amend the Railway Act.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
We discussed this matter several weeks ago and as Mr. Speaker was putting the question to the 57 i
House for the second reading, the Prime Minister asked that it should stand. 1 spoke twice on the measure; everybody spoke who wanted to, and then the Minister of Railways said that if I allowed the Bill to stand, he might have a suggestion to make in a day or two. Two Bills which we have been considering to-day got precedence over it, although this had precedence in the beginning. The matter having been thoroughly discussed, I think the Bill ought to go to committee, and I would move to that effect.
Mr.^ GRAHAM. This Bill is one that in short provides that every coroner should-hold an inquest when any death occurs that is caused by a railway. The position I took the other day was that the coroners are not our employees, but employees of the provincial governments and paid by them. I do not deny that this House can use the officers of the provincial government if it wants to, but we cannot compel them to do something that their oath of office as employees of the provincial government prohibits them from doing. Now, take the statutes of the different provinces. Under the Nova Scotia Act a coroner cannot hold an inquest until it appears:
(a)	That there is reasonable cause to suspect that such person died from violence, undue means or culpable negligence, or
(b)	That such person died in any- jail or in any prison, or
(c)	That such person died in such place and under such circumstances as require an inquest.
It is further provided that every person appointed a coroner shall hold office during pleasure, and shall before entering upon the duties of his office take an oath. This would not interfere to any extent with this Bill. But in New Brunswick it is provided that the coroner shall not be entitled to his fees unless prior to issuing his warrant for summoning a jury he makes a declaration under oath that he is of opinion that there is reason for believing or suspecting that the deceased did not come to his death by mere natural causes or from mere accident or mischance, but came to his death by violence, criminal or unfair means, culpable or negligent conduct of others under circumstances requiring investigation by a coroner's inquest, and the grounds on which he bases such belief or suspicion must be set out. Our law might conflict with this. In Quebec coroners are governed by section 3477 of the Revised Statutes of 1906, which says:
No inquest shall be held on any deceased person unless a coroner before issuing his warrant for summoning a jury makes an affidavit administered by a justice of the peace, notary public or a commissioner for taking affidavits to be used in the Superior Court, and filed with the inquisition, stating that

from the information received by the coroner, a summary whereof shall Toe sent out in the declaration, he has reason for believing that the deceased came to his death not from natural causes or mere accident or mischance, but from violence or unfair means, culpable or negligent conduct of others under circumstances requiring investigation by a coroner's inquest.
It might be apparent, that no person was culpable, and yet we would require him to do what under the provincial statutes he is not required to do and what he swears he will not do. Chap. 97 of the Revised Statutes of Ontario, 1897, provides that: No inquest shall be held on the body of any deceased person by a coroner unless it be upon the death of a prisoner or upon the written request of the Attorney General in certain cases, unless it has been made to appear to the coroner that there is reason to believe that the deceased died from violence or unfair means by culpable or negligent conduct of others and under such circumstances as require investigation by inquest and not through mere accident or mischance. Then, section 4 provides that no fee shall be payable to the coroner unless prior to issuing his warrant for the summoning of the jury he makes a declaration under oath stating that from information received by him he is of opinion that there is reason to believe that the deceased did not come to his death from natural causes or from mere accident or mischance, but came to his death From violence or unfair means or culpable or negligent conduct of others under circumstances requiring investigation by coroner's inquest. By the Manitoba Act it is provided that no fees shall be claimed by a coroner unless prior to issuing his warrant for summoning a jury he shall have made a declaration in writing under oath stating that from information received he is of opinion that there is reason to believe that the deceased did not come to his death from natural causes or from mere accident or mischance, but came to his death from violence or unfair means or culpable or negligent conduct of others requiring investigation by a coroner's inquest. The British Columbia Act, I think, would not possibly interfere with the proposition of my hon. friend, because under that Act where a coroner is informed that a dead body of a person is lying within his jurisdiction, and there is reasonable cause to suspect that such person died either a violent or unnatural death or has died a sudden death the cause of which is unknown under such circumstances as to require an inquest, he shall issue his warrant for summoning a jury. My contention is that as coroners are employees of the provincial government, which defines their duties, though we can use these officials, we cannot require them to do something which may conflict with their Mr. GRAHAM.
instructions or with the oath they have to take. I would have no hesitation in saying that we might compel every railway company, where a fatal accident has occurred, to at once report to the nearest coroner or the Crown Attorney, or the Attorney General, as the case might be, and leave him to decide whether or not to hold an investigation, but I think we shall be going beyond what is warranted by the statutes of all the provinces if we require an inquest to be held where under the circumstances it might not be necessary. I would be quite willing to send the Bill to the Railway Committee to be there threshed out, but I think it would be a mistake for us as a parliament to compel the officers of the provincial government to do something which would be manifestly contrary to the oath they have to take from their employers.

speechtext: I would like to point out that in the province of Quebec the coroners are paid by the provincial government, and it is in the discretion of the government, if they do not comply with the provisions of the law, to refuse payment. .If we required these men to perform certain work for which the provincial government refused to pay them, it is probable that they would refuse to act.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
It is very easy to find excuses for not passing legislation. On the second reading of this Bill every one who spoke was in favour of it on its merits. The reasons given by the Minister of Railways and Canals with regard to these provincial statutes are the very reasons why this parliament should take some action. Our railways to-day are almost entirely Dominion railways, with regard to which this parliament alone can legislate, and we are never troubled in so legislating by the fact that some provincial act affecting these railways may be in existence. There are provincial Acts governing our coroners, yet the Criminal Code of this parliament provides that they shall perform certain duties. If a man is supposed to be guilty in a case of death, he is taken into custody by the coroner holding an inquest. In our criminal code there are dozens of instances in which magistrates and justices of the peace, who are appointed by the local governments, must act. One might as well say that a county court judge, because he is appointed by this government, must not enforce any provincial law. County court judges are appointed and paid for by the Dominion government, but in nine cases out of ten they deal with matters of provincial legislation only. Of course I anticipated these objections. Counsels for different railways have told me that there objections would, be raised, and in all probability the objec-

tions raised by the hon. minister came from the railway companies.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Counsel for these companies told me what was going to be urged on the second reading of this Bill. They said that the position would be taken which we have seen taken in this House to-day. The coroner would be loaded up behind the backs of the relatives and the public so that, under the law governing Dominion railways he could say that he had made an inquiry and that in his opinion no inquest was necessary, and no provincial law could provide for anything being done on the property of a Dominion railway.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That is no answer.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is an answer as strong as your argument.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That may be the opinion of the hon. gentleman, and he is welcome to it; but in the Railway Commission over and over again it has been decided that this parliament alone can deal with these matters.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman contend that a provincial government cannot, through its coroners, have anything to do with the death of a person because it occurred on a Dominion railway?

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I have not said that. My Bill provides that where these deaths occur on the property of a Dominion railway, certain things should be done, and the section I am amending enacts that the Railway Commission shall do certain things in certain cases. Will the hon. minister say that the Railway Commission must get the sanction of a provincial government before it can carry out its powers? He certainly will not because he wants the Railway Commission to have these powers, but he pretends that we must not enact that a coroner must do anything because forsooth we would thereby be interfering with provincial jurisdiction. I am asking that the coroner be bound to inquire and ascertain the causes of death in certain cases. Everybody knows how these deaths, instead of diminishing, are increasing, and we all know that if the responsible parties are not brought to book, this condition of things will continue. Of course if the minister is determined that the House shall not deal with this, he is in control, and there is no use of my wasting time in discussing the matter, but I submit that the proper place to deal with this Bill is in Committee of the Whole House, just as we have dealt with the Bill we have been discussing previous to this one, and with the Bill on interest. The latter was a measure which might, much more properly have been referred to a standing committee, but nevertheless it was dealt with by this House in Committee of the Whole, and similar treatment should certainly be given this much more important measure.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
Mr. GRAHAM moved that the Bill be referred to the standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.
Motion agreed to.
